title: The One-Buyer Problem: Why a Single Interested Party Rarely Pays What Your Business Is Worth
linkedin:
An unsolicited approach to buy your business feels like validation the moment it lands. A competitor calls, a private equity associate mentions it in passing, a long-time supplier says they would buy the place tomorrow. The instinct is to take that interest seriously and start talking.

Here is the pattern we see consistently across owner-led businesses in Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne. A business that talks to one interested party almost always settles for a lower price and more buyer-friendly terms than one that creates genuine competing interest first. It is not about the buyer acting unfairly. It is simply what happens to leverage when only one side of the table has options.

Without a second party in the picture, a buyer's opening number tends to become the ceiling of the negotiation, not the floor. Due diligence can drag longer than it needs to. Small issues get raised as reasons to revisit the price. The seller, having mentally moved on from the business, finds it harder to walk away at month four than it would have been at week one.

None of this requires turning a private decision into a public sale process. A small number of genuinely qualified parties approached quietly in parallel is usually enough to change the entire dynamic, including how firmly a buyer holds their first number.

Ever had someone approach you out of the blue about buying your business? A competitor, a supplier, someone at an industry event?

It feels flattering, and the instinct is to just talk to that one person and see where it goes. But we see this pattern constantly: a business talking to a single interested buyer almost always ends up with a lower price and less favourable terms than one that has even two or three genuinely interested parties in the mix.

It is not that the buyer is being unfair. They just have no reason to move off their first number when there is no one else in the room.
